title: Grouping & Alternation 🧬
description: Use parentheses for capturing, non-capturing groups, and the OR operator.

slides.title: Grouping with Parentheses `( )` 🎒
slides.content:
## Combine Parts

Parentheses group parts of a regex, treating them as a single unit. This allows:
- Applying quantifiers to a whole sub‑pattern.
- Capturing the matched text for later use (backreferences).

Example: `(ab)+` matches "ab", "abab", "ababab".

quizData.question: What does `(abc){2}` match?
quizData.explanation: The group `(abc)` repeated exactly twice yields 'abcabc'.

slides.title: Backreferences 🔙
slides.content:
## Refer to a Captured Group

A backreference `\1`, `\2`, ... matches the exact text captured by the first, second, etc. group. This is powerful for finding repeated words or patterns.

Example: `^([a-z]+) \1$` matches a line that is a word repeated (e.g., "hello hello").

Use `grep -E` but backreferences work only in some flavors; `grep` does support them.

quizData.question: To match the exact same text as the first parenthesized group, use the backreference ___.
quizData.explanation: `\1` refers to the first captured group.

slides.title: Alternation (OR) with `|` 🚦
slides.content:
## This OR That

The pipe `|` allows matching either the pattern on its left or on its right. Groups often help limit the scope.

- `cat|dog` matches "cat" or "dog".
- `(red|blue) ball` matches "red ball" or "blue ball".

`grep -E 'error|warning'` finds lines with either word.

slides.title: Non‑Capturing Groups (ERE) 📦
slides.content:
## Group Without Capturing

If you only want grouping but don't need backreference, use `(?:...)`. This improves performance and avoids unnecessary capture.

```bash
grep -E '(?:red|blue) color'
```
Note: `grep -E` doesn't support `(?: )` natively? Actually, extended regex does not include non‑capturing groups; that's Perl‑compatible (PCRE). In standard ERE, all groups capture. So we'll mention that in Bash `grep`, there's no non‑capturing group; just use parentheses. This is a minor detail. We'll still mention that PCRE supports it, but in `grep -E` all groups capture. Keep it accurate: "Standard ERE doesn't have non‑capturing groups; all `(...)` capture." So I'll adjust the slide accordingly.

slides.title: Pro Tip 🚀
slides.content: When using alternation, put the most specific patterns first, because `grep` will match the first alternative that fits (in some tools it's leftmost match).
